headline: Ironic framework brings enterprise architecture to Rust, simplifying large backend apps
summary: Ironic is a new Rust framework designed to simplify enterprise backend development, offering modularity and conventions for large applications while preserving Rust's unique compile-time guarantees and ownership model.
details: Ironic is a new Rust framework designed to simplify enterprise backend development. It aims to make large Rust applications easier to organize and maintain, addressing challenges faced by projects that evolve over several years.

The framework tackles the problem of inconsistent project organization in Rust, where powerful primitives often lead to teams reinventing solutions. Ironic provides conventions to streamline development processes.

Unlike some frameworks that abstract away language specifics, Ironic embraces Rust's philosophy. It uses procedural macros and compile-time code generation, preserving the ownership model rather than replacing it with runtime magic.
Ironic encourages applications to be organized around modules, keeping business logic cohesive instead of scattered. This approach helps manage complexity as projects grow.

The framework's design prioritizes developer experience and long-term maintainability over chasing marginal performance gains. It focuses on reducing infrastructure wiring so engineers can concentrate on business logic.

This initiative represents a step towards improving the developer experience for large Rust applications, ensuring they remain maintainable without sacrificing the unique qualities of the Rust language.
Still evolving, Ironic's design decisions are rooted in repeatedly solving real-world production system problems. It seeks to remove unnecessary repetition while embracing Rust's strengths.
The creator invites feedback and contributions from developers interested in modular Rust backends, distributed systems, and enterprise application architecture to help the ecosystem grow.

headline_marked: [[Updated Android app from a restaurant]] with laptop off, using a home PC as a remote dev server
headline: Updated Android app from a restaurant with laptop off, using a home PC as a remote dev server
summary: A developer leveraged a home Ubuntu PC with a coding agent and remote SSH to update an Android app from his phone, demonstrating persistent remote development without a local laptop.
details: The author updated an Expo Android app from his phone using a coding agent (Codex) while his MacBook Air was off in a restaurant. The development environment, including the repository, backend, database, and build tools, ran on an old Ubuntu gaming PC at home. He saw the changes immediately on his phone.

This setup was initially built for efficient hardware use, but revealed a new paradigm: "local development" was happening remotely. The home PC, a modest Ryzen 5 5600G with 16 GB RAM and 1 TB storage, was repurposed from gaming, not specifically bought for AI agents.

An earlier attempt with Windows, WSL, Docker, and remote desktop on the MacBook was awkward, consuming too much memory for the environment itself. Switching to Ubuntu on the tower allowed the home PC to focus on codebases, Docker, databases, servers, builds, and agents.

The MacBook Air now functions as the client, running VS Code, Codex, and browser, while the Ubuntu tower handles OpenSSH, Docker, PostgreSQL, backend/frontend servers, Metro, and Android builds. Tailscale creates a private network for secure OpenSSH connections.

VS Code Remote SSH allows the MacBook to access the Ubuntu repository as if local, with the integrated terminal and extensions running on the tower. Port forwarding exposes development servers on the MacBook's localhost, simplifying access without remembering private addresses.

This setup provides a persistent development environment; closing the MacBook doesn't stop ongoing tasks. The home PC acts as infrastructure, running continuously for weeks, allowing the author to launch work and return to it later from any client without rebuilding the environment.

This persistence offers a benefit beyond a simple hardware upgrade. A more powerful laptop would compile faster, but wouldn't provide the continuous, always-on development environment that the dedicated remote server does.
